newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish police pledge crackdown on drugs.
newsitem.headline: Polish police pledge crackdown on drugs.

text.p: The Polish police declared war on drug dealers and smugglers on Tuesday to cut major international drug trafficking routes and prevent the country from becoming a marketplace for narcotics.
"Drug abuses and crime related to them are rising steeply..., we must take tough measures against that," recently appointed police chief Marek Papala told a news conference.

He said international drug cartels were using Poland as a transit route for drugs being smuggled into western Europe and the United States from South America, Asia and Africa, and dealers were beginning to penetrate schools and universities.
"The situation is getting beyond the level of society's tolerance," he said.

Papala said he had decided to create a special narcotics bureau in the police force to coordinate the efforts of other state institutions, such as the security police and the border guard, in the fight against drug-related crime.
The bureau will cooperate closely with Interpol and police in Western countries and will use techniques such as "sting" actions, telephone tapping and undercover agents, he said.

Papala pledged the bureau, initially employing 400 officers, would not lack funds despite the Polish police force's meagre budget. "The money for this purpose must be found and will be found," he said.

One of the bureau's priorities would be to liquidate laboratories manufacturing amphetamines, of which Poland is Europe's major supplier, he said. "Some of these facilities are really factories and not laboratories..., which employ high-class chemistry experts," he said, adding that Polish amphetamine was popular in the West because of its purity.

Poland has seen a steep rise in drug consumption and trafficking since the fall of communism in 1989, when travel restrictions were liberalised and police powers, often abused under communism, were curbed.

The number of officially registered drug addicts jumped to nearly 20,000 last year from about 14,000 in 1990 as new drugs -- heroin, cocaine, amphetamine, marijuana and LSD -- began to replace the contaminated, home-made poppy-seed extract known as "kompot."
Last year, police and border guards detected 97 cases of cross-border drug smuggling, 28 more than in 1995. "But all this is just the tip of an iceberg," Papala said.
